standard.title: Soils, Rocks and Minerals
standard.description: compare the observable properties of soils, rocks and minerals and investigate why they are important Earth resources
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can observe and describe properties of natural and made materials (AC9SFU03, F band). They have not yet systematically compared soil types, distinguished rocks from minerals, or examined Earth materials as resources that living things depend on.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students compare observable properties of soils, rocks and minerals using appropriate vocabulary, understand that minerals are components of rocks, and explain why soils, rocks and minerals are important resources for living things including humans.

nodes.label: Soils have observable properties and components
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can describe the observable components of soil samples (pebbles, sand, clay, plant matter, living things) and compare the properties of different soils using observable evidence.
nodes.minimum_width: Students examine at least two soil samples, identify their components, and describe at least two observable differences between them.
nodes.typical_width: Students examine soils from different local contexts, describe components and properties (particle size, colour, texture, water retention, presence of organic matter), compare soils systematically, and explain how soil properties affect its suitability for plant growth.
wider: Investigate how farmers use soil tests to monitor and manage farm health — connecting observable soil properties to agricultural decision-making (AC9S3H01)
Examine information on plant tags and explore vocabulary used to describe soil requirements — applying property knowledge to real plant care contexts
Explore how First Nations Australians observe soil and landscape characteristics to make decisions about resource availability and land management

response_modes.reason: Students need to accumulate accurate observations across multiple soil samples using consistent property vocabulary before they can compare or explain differences. Without a shared property vocabulary, comparisons are vague ('this soil is better') rather than evidence-based ('this soil has finer particles and holds more water').

success_criteria: Identifies at least three components in a soil sample using observation
Compares two soil samples using at least two property terms with observable evidence

nodes.label: Rocks and minerals have observable properties
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can describe and compare observable properties of rocks and minerals (colour, texture, grain size, crystal size, hardness, lustre), and explain that minerals are the building blocks of rocks.
nodes.minimum_width: Students describe at least two observable properties of each of three different rock or mineral samples, and state that minerals are components of rocks.
nodes.typical_width: Students compare rocks and minerals systematically using property vocabulary, explain that rocks are composed of one or more minerals, identify similarities and differences between samples from local and non-local sources, and recognise common uses of minerals.
wider: Investigate First Nations Australians' knowledge of different rock and mineral types and how they were used — for stone blades, grindstones and pigments — examining how deep property knowledge guided material selection
Explore the school grounds or local area to observe and collect different rock types and construct a comparative display showing property differences
Research which rocks or minerals are quarried or mined locally and how they are used — connecting local geology to community resources

response_modes.reason: Students commonly have a narrow rock concept (grey, hard, outdoor) and miss the diversity of rock and mineral types in their environment. Encountering a range of samples — including minerals with vivid colour, crystal structure, or varied hardness — builds a more accurate and complete model of what rocks and minerals are.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: First Nations knowledge of rock and mineral properties for tool-making provides a sophisticated real-world application of property-based selection that connects geological knowledge to human practice. Local quarrying and mining research grounds the abstract concept of 'Earth resource' in the student's community context.
success_criteria: Describes at least two observable properties for each of three rock or mineral samples
Explains that minerals are the building blocks of rocks

nodes.label: Soils, rocks and minerals are important Earth resources
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain why soils, rocks and minerals are important resources for living things — including how living things depend on soils and how humans use rocks and minerals — and give specific examples of each.
nodes.minimum_width: Students give at least two examples of how living things depend on soil and at least two examples of how humans use rocks or minerals, explaining why each is important.
nodes.typical_width: Students explain the multiple ways living things depend on soils (food production, plant growth, habitat, water filtration) and describe how humans use specific rocks and minerals in everyday objects and the built environment, connecting specific properties to specific uses.
wider: Investigate which rocks or minerals are quarried or mined locally or regionally and examine how those resources are used — tracing the resource from extraction to use
Research how humans depend on soils for food production and examine what happens when soil quality degrades — connecting soil health to food security
Examine how First Nations Australians' use of rocks, minerals and soils reflects a deep understanding of their properties and sustainable use within Country

response_modes.reason: Students commonly think of soil as 'dirt' and miss its ecological and agricultural importance. Encountering the multiple roles of soil — habitat, water filtration, food production, plant support — and varied uses of rocks and minerals across the built environment and everyday objects builds a more complete understanding of Earth materials as resources.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Local quarrying/mining research and First Nations sustainable use provide genuinely rich directions that connect the abstract concept of 'Earth resource' to specific community and cultural contexts. The soil degradation direction introduces a real-world consequence that motivates the importance of soil health.
success_criteria: Gives at least two examples of how living things depend on soil with explanation
Gives at least two examples of human use of rocks or minerals, connecting the use to a property of the material
